2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern / largely not applicable — Cross-sectional qualitative fieldwork with high participation: all approached respondents except one agreed to participate across 81 completed interviews and group discussions (PDF p. 6, Section 2.2), and there was no longitudinal follow-up cohort.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable as a causal-inference estimator (non-comparative qualitative political-economy case study) — The study does not estimate quantitative causal treatment effects, though it explicitly maps contextual and institutional factors (historical Ujamaa campaigns, fiscal centralization, delayed transfers, per diem incentives, and weak village solidarity networks) shaping implementation (PDF pp. 4-8, Sections 2.1 and 3.1-3.3).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Clearly identifies and distinguishes relevant Tanzanian policy and administrative governance instruments (1998 Policy Paper on Local Government Reform, 2010 inter-ministerial MoU, 2011 Draft Sanitation and Hygiene Policy, 2012 NSC Concept Note, intergovernmental transfer rules including the unimplemented 20% district-to-village revenue share, and public-sector per diem rules), separating de jure mandates from de facto local bureaucratic practice, though relying on policy/grey documents without granular statutory citations (PDF pp. 6-10, Sections 3.1-3.2 and 4.1-4.2).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern — Interviews were conducted mostly in Swahili using handwritten notes compared within the team prior to transcription rather than audio recordings, no semi-structured interview guide is provided, and researcher/NGO positionality is not examined (PDF p. 6, Section 2.2; p. 14, Acknowledgments). In addition, the authors document high error rates in routine village-collected NSC baseline questionnaires (40% significantly wrong in their non-representative field check; PDF p. 11, Section 4.3).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak for household sanitation outcomes (process-focused governance study) — Primary empirical focus is institutional process across five management functions rather than household sanitation outcomes; no independent representative measurement of latrine construction or ODF status is conducted, and audited administrative baseline surveys exhibited severe error (estimated 25% failure rate by district staff and 40% significant error in checked forms; PDF p. 11, Section 4.3).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern — Results systematically report across all five pre-specified project management functions (Planning, Budgeting, Coordination, Implementation, Monitoring; Tables 1-2, PDF pp. 5, 9-12), including unfavorable findings, but absence of transparent coding rules, district-by-district disaggregation (e.g., comparing high- vs low-performing sampled districts), and verbatim participant quotations limits auditability against selective narrative synthesis.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern — Purposive district sampling intentionally spanned performance tiers (6 of 42 NSC districts combining initially outstanding, regular, and low performance) and included 81 interviews/group discussions across national, regional, district, ward, and village levels (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2), but criteria for choosing the 3 regions, 9 wards, 15 villages, and 'random villagers' who attended triggering are unreported, and districts themselves avoided very isolated or culturally challenging communities in Year 1 (PDF p. 9, Section 4.1).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its aim to examine the role, capacities, motivations, and constraints of decentralized local government authorities (district councils) in rural sanitation promotion under Tanzania's National Sanitation Campaign (NSC) across planning, budgeting, coordination, implementation, and monitoring, and to propose adjustments for a more effective service delivery model.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF p. 1 (Abstract); PDF p. 3 (Section 1.1); PDF pp. 4-5 (Section 2.1, Table 1)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative governance and political economy approach using semi-structured interviews, group discussions, and policy review is well suited to investigating institutional incentives, bureaucratic accountability, village-level social dynamics, and operational bottlenecks in decentralized sanitation promotion.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify applying the three-step Problem-Driven Governance and Political Economy (PGPE) framework (structural factors, institutions, and actors) to a multi-tier case study of the NSC across five core district management functions aligned with national policy mandates.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Purposive sampling of 6 out of 42 NSC-implementing districts deliberately combined initially outstanding, regular, and low performers, and captured 81 interviews/group discussions across national ministries/stakeholders (12), regions (8), districts (26), and wards/villages (35, including elected leaders, executive officers, NGOs/CBOs, health workers, follow-up committees, masons, and villagers), with non-participation reported (1 refusal). Sub-district selection procedures for the 15 villages and 'random villagers' are only briefly summarized.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection combined policy and grey-literature review with 81 semi-structured interviews, group discussions, and key informant consultations during the first financial year of NSC implementation (mid-2012 to mid-2013), conducted mostly in Swahili with field notes compared across the research team prior to transcription, plus field checks of village action plans and baseline questionnaires. However, no interview guide, audio-recording rationale, or discussion of data saturation is provided.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Although confidentiality was promised to encourage candid opinions, the authors provide no reflexive discussion of their own positionality, institutional affiliations, or how operational support from sector NGOs (WaterAid and ONGAWA) and donor-funded consortia (SHARE/DFID) may have shaped access, framing, or respondent candour across ministry, district, and village interviews.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors report that all participants were clearly informed of the research purpose beforehand, participation was voluntary (all except one agreed), and individual confidentiality was granted. However, there is no mention of formal institutional ethics committee / IRB review or whether consent was written or oral, leaving ethical oversight partially unclear.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: While deductive PGPE categories and five project management functions structure the inquiry (Table 1) and interview notes were compared within the team before transcription, the paper provides no explanation of coding procedures, thematic synthesis, how divergent perspectives across high- versus low-performing districts were reconciled, or verbatim participant quotations to substantiate analytical claims.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized and synthesized across historical/institutional context (Sections 3.1-3.3) and each of the five NSC project management functions across government tiers (Table 2; Sections 4.1-4.4), directly answering the research question regarding which functions suit district direct execution versus external support, despite lacking direct respondent quotes.

Narrative assessment: High practical and policy value. The study explains concrete institutional mechanisms behind disappointing scaled-up CLTS and sanitation marketing results in Tanzania (centralized project budgeting, 6-month transfer delays, staff per diem distortions absorbing ~45% of district budgets, untrained unpaid village committees, unviable rural mason supply chains, and lack of community safety nets for vulnerable households) and offers actionable recommendations for balancing local government oversight, equity monitoring, and outsourced facilitation across Sub-Saharan Africa.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable (high policy and operational relevance; narrative item)

evidence_quotes.quote: In our case, the methodology is applied to a specific project: the NSC in Tanzania.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Sample size of qualitative interviews and group discussions (CASP Q4, Q5)
evidence_quotes.quote: In total, 81 interviews or group discussions were carried out.

evidence_quotes.quote: Information was obtained from three regions, six districts, nine wards and 15 villages.

evidence_quotes.quote: Most of the interviews were held in Swahili. Notes were taken during each interview

evidence_quotes.quote: no visits to communities will take place if the per diem is not secured.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Jiménez, Mtango, and Cairncross (2014) present a primary qualitative multi-tier governance and political economy case study of local government roles during the first year (2012-2013) of Tanzania's National Sanitation Campaign (NSC). Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study demonstrates clear aims (Q1: Yes), an appropriate qualitative PGPE framework and multi-level design (Q2: Yes; Q3: Yes), purposive multi-tier recruitment across 6 districts of varying initial performance totaling 81 interviews and group discussions with only one refusal (Q4: Yes), structured multi-source field data collection (Q5: Yes), clear synthesis of findings across five project management functions (Q9: Yes), and strong policy value (Q10). Methodological concerns center on three areas (1 No and 2 Can't tell items): complete absence of researcher reflexivity regarding author/NGO/donor positionality (Q6: No), partial ethical reporting that notes informed purpose, voluntary participation, and confidentiality without mentioning institutional ethics committee approval (Q7: Can't tell), and opaque qualitative data analysis procedures relying on unquoted field notes without documented coding, inter-district comparison, or verbatim participant quotations (Q8: Can't tell). Overall methodological concern is Moderate.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 No and 2 Can't tell items out of Q1-Q9)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative multi-tier case study using Problem-Driven Governance and Political Economy (PGPE) analysis (81 semi-structured interviews and group discussions across national, regional, district, ward, and village levels, plus policy and grey-literature review)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research aims and rationale in Abstract (PDF p. 1), Section 1.1 (PDF p. 3), and Section 2.1 (PDF pp. 4-5, Table 1); sampling, data collection, consent/confidentiality, and note-taking in Section 2.2 (PDF pp. 5-6); institutional and legal-administrative context in Sections 3.1-3.3 (PDF pp. 6-8); NSC functional findings and field questionnaire check in Sections 4.1-4.4 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 8-12); policy implications, conclusions, and funding/NGO acknowledgments in Sections 5-6 and Acknowledgments (PDF pp. 12-14).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's empirical design (Section 2, PDF pp. 4-6) is a primary qualitative field case study based on 81 semi-structured interviews and group discussions across four administrative tiers in 6 purposively sampled Tanzanian districts, supplemented by policy/document review. There is no quantitative experimental/quasi-experimental comparator or statistical analysis (brief descriptive budget figures and a non-representative field check of baseline forms serve only to contextualize qualitative implementation findings), making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the matching tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
